text: Three weeks after Lesson 30's guardrails went in, Meridian's ops team launches a third instance, meridian-web2, to handle an unexpected traffic bump, and nobody on the team can SSH into it. It's a plain connectivity problem, not a budget or security incident, and it gets worked the same methodical way every time: instance state first, then public IP, then security group, then route table, strictly in that order.

describe-instances shows the instance state as running, which rules out a crashed or still-booting instance before anyone even opens a security group. The same command's PublicIpAddress field comes back null, though — meridian-web2 has no public IP address at all, which means no amount of security group tuning will ever let SSH reach it from Meridian's office network.

SubnetId tells the real story: meridian-web2 landed in subnet-0meridianpriv, the private subnet from Lesson 29, not the public one it was meant for. Someone on the ops team copy-pasted the app tier's subnet ID from an old command in their shell history instead of the web tier's. That subnet never had map-public-ip-on-launch turned on and has no route to an internet gateway — the two things Lesson 29 said make a subnet actually public.

describe-route-tables on that subnet still gets checked, as a matter of discipline, and comes back clean — only a local route, no path to an internet gateway, confirming the route table was never the thing to fix here. The root cause is the subnet choice itself at launch time, not a missing rule anywhere downstream of it.

An EC2 instance's subnet can't be changed after launch, so the fix is terminate-instances followed by a fresh run-instances pointed at subnet-0meridianpub with associate-public-ip-address set correctly this time. Meridian's ops team also adopts Systems Manager Session Manager for admin access going forward — no open port 22, no public IP required at all, and this entire category of mistake stops being possible.
